articles.title: Slothshot: it sorts your screenshots overnight, and it will never delete one
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3, Slow and Steady. Slothshot sorts the screenshots piling up on your computer while you are not using it. Overnight, while th…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3 , Slow and Steady. What I built Slothshot sorts the screenshots piling up on your computer while you are not using it. Overnight, while the laptop is idle and plugged in, entirely offline, on Windows, macOS and Linux. You have hundreds of files called Screenshot 2026-08-04 at 6.00.00 p.m..png . You know one of them has the booking number. Finding it means opening them one at a time. An open-weight vision model reads each one on your own machine , gives it a name you can recognise, files it by what it is, and leaves a Review pile for the duplicates and the things that have expired.
articles.author: Marco Ramírez

articles.title: Make a Nuxt or Next.js site readable by AI: llms.txt, robots.txt, Markdown
articles.excerpt: Ask an AI assistant about a page on your site and one of three things happens. It answers from what it learned in training, it answers from a search index it built earlier, or it fetches your page rig…
articles.body: Ask an AI assistant about a page on your site and one of three things happens. It answers from what it learned in training, it answers from a search index it built earlier, or it fetches your page right now. In all three, a crawler read your HTML at some point. What it was allowed to read, and how easily, is the part you can shape. I built four pieces for that into the SEO plugin of Easy CMS, my embedded CMS for Nuxt and Next.js ( the first post in this series introduces it). The ideas work in any server-rendered site: robots.txt rules for AI crawlers, by what they do. /llms.txt , a short Markdown index of the site, and /llms-full.txt , the whole site in one file. A Markdown URL for each page, such as /posts/hello.md . IndexNow pings when a page changes for visitors.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady. I have been lowkey falling behind my lectures. I start each semester with a burning motivation to pay atten…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady . What I Built I have been lowkey falling behind my lectures. I start each semester with a burning motivation to pay attention in class. BUT writing notes is just too damn tiresome, especially when I also need to pay attention to what my professors are saying. Because let's be honest, once they go off on a tangent, I have no clue what the hell they just said. AND for some reason, none of them ever record their lectures despite it being compulsory for them 🫩. HOWEVER, for International Sloth Day, I decided to just make an app that takes my phone recordings and makes notes for me, so I don't have to do the hard work 😄. And that's how LazyNotes came about.

articles.title: Node.js Audio Transcription: Preserving Structured CRM Actions Through Retries
articles.excerpt: A transcription worker should treat audio transcription as an unreliable boundary, not as the place where CRM writes happen. Put that boundary behind a durable job, persist the source and an idempoten…
articles.body: A transcription worker should treat audio transcription as an unreliable boundary, not as the place where CRM writes happen. Put that boundary behind a durable job, persist the source and an idempotency key, validate the returned text, and let a separate action step produce and apply structured CRM changes. Retries then repeat a replaceable artifact instead of creating duplicate tasks, contacts, or follow-ups. Short answer: in a Node.js service, call transcription through a small adapter, store the transcript with a content hash, and make every downstream CRM mutation conditional on a stable call ID. The endpoint is configuration; retry and commit rules belong to your system. This is the difference between transcribing a sales call and safely turning that call into CRM work.

articles.body: Seeding a database with user1 , user2 , test@test.com works right up until your UI has to render a real-looking name, your demo needs 500 believable products, or your test suite needs the same dataset on every run, not a fresh snowflake each time. SynthForge is a synthetic data API we built at DSP to fix that. It's live on RapidAPI with a free tier. Predefined generators Seven generators, up to 1,000 records per call : person , company , address , product , user , payment-card , and internet , covering names, safe emails, phones, job titles, SKUs, prices, usernames, IPs, UUIDs, and the rest of the usual test-data furniture.

articles.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 was malware. A 5-minute check for AI developers, and the one-line setting that would have skipped it
articles.excerpt: On October 21, 2026, a malicious litellm==1.107.0 was published to PyPI. It is the second compromise of the package this year, separate from the one in March. PyPI has removed it. The safe version is…
articles.body: On October 21, 2026, a malicious litellm==1.107.0 was published to PyPI. It is the second compromise of the package this year, separate from the one in March. PyPI has removed it. The safe version is 1.106.2 . LiteLLM is the library many agents and proxies use to call Claude, GPT and other models through one interface. It often arrives as a dependency you never installed on purpose. And this payload goes after AI coding tool credentials by name : Claude, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI and others. The best technical analysis so far is the write-up by GMO Flatt Security (in Japanese). This post summarizes it for an English-speaking audience and adds the part I couldn't find elsewhere: how to make your installer refuse brand-new releases.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
articles.excerpt: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's…
articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
